about_us_title: Project Bruut: By and for the community
about_us_intro: Robotics in agriculture is often complex and unaffordable. We believe this can be different. Project Bruut was born from the desire to design a modular, open-source field robot that you, as a farmer or maker, can build, understand, and adapt yourself.
about_us_opensource_text: We want to make complex robotics accessible by providing a solid foundation. Because the project is open-source, you are not tied to expensive licenses or closed ecosystems. You have the freedom to fully customize the tool carrier to your own needs and share your innovations with others.
about_us_independence_text: No unnecessary electronics or overly complex systems. We use as many off-the-shelf standard components as possible. This means the robot is easy to build and, more importantly, that you can repair it yourself in the field without having to wait for an expensive technician.
about_us_reality_text: Let’s be honest: robotics is difficult. So don’t expect a ready-made commercial product wrapped up with a bow. What we do offer is a robust, programmable frame and a clear manual. We give you the tool—you give the robot its purpose.
about_us_community_text: Whether you’re a farmer with a welding machine or a developer who enjoys working with Ardupilot—we do this together. How great is it to share ideas as a community of enthusiasts, improve them, test them in the mud, and simply use them together?
about_us_conclusion: Help build the future of accessible agricultural robotics. Share your attachments, improve the code, or simply start building your own Bruut.

front_page_info_platform_title: Building the Future of Field Robotics
front_page_info_platform_desc: Project BRUUT is an initiative started by Jan Jaap Verweij, a Dutch dairy farmer and lead contributor to the open-source projects Cowcatcher and CalvingCatcher, where computer vision is transforming dairy farming; building on experience in software and electronics, the project expands into robotics to develop a simple, autonomous field robot that addresses key agricultural challenges such as reducing chemical use, lowering fuel and machinery costs, tackling labor shortages, and improving sustainability through applications like spot spraying, mechanical weed control, soil health improvement, and support for physically demanding work.
front_page_media_desc: A simple, affordable, and highly customizable solution. Whether you are a dairy farmer, arable farmer, or grow vegetables in greenhouses or in open fields, this tool carrier robot can be adapted to suit your needs and work seamlessly with 'community' or own machines.
front_page_feature_1_desc: No unnecessary electronics. Built with standard parts for easy maintenance, repairs, and expansion.
front_page_feature_2_desc: Adjustable width and length via a hole-bar system. Scalable for open fields, greenhouses, or gardens.
front_page_feature_3_desc: Scalable power from 400W to 5kW. Choose between 2-wheel or 4-wheel drive for maximum traction.
front_page_stats_subtitle: The modular power of open-source farming.
front_page_youtube_desc: Everything that happens to Bruut ends up on YouTube: welding the chassis, wiring the motor controllers, the first autonomous rows and the tests that went wrong. It is the fastest way to follow the project and to see exactly how the robot is put together.

func_hero_subtitle: The Bruut platform is a versatile tool carrier. Discover all modules and attachments you can add for specific tasks in the field, greenhouse, or yard.
func_1_desc: Front-mounted or mid-mounted between the front and rear wheels. Usable as a grader for leveling terrain, for pushing feed and grass back in the stable, or for cleaning silos.
func_2_desc: Trencher for digging wet buffer strips and drainage ditches, so standing water is carried off the field efficiently.
func_3_desc: Compact cultivator for soil cultivation in vegetable gardens and light plots.
func_4_desc: Hoeing unit with single-axis (left/right) guidance that stays tightly between the rows, for example in maize, so weeds are cut close to the crop without damaging it.
func_5_desc: Mechanical weed control using rotating fingers in light soil.
func_6_desc: Front-mounted boom with conventional high-pressure nozzles that atomise the liquid into a fine mist. Each nozzle is switched individually, so only the detected weed is treated while the fine droplets fully cover the leaf surface. Based on the 'Open Weed Locator' project and ideal for contact herbicides and crop protection products.
func_7_desc: Boom with individually controlled injectors that fire single coarse droplets on demand at low pressure. Every droplet is placed straight onto the weed, which practically eliminates drift and cuts chemical usage to a fraction of a conventional spray pass.
func_8_desc: Two-axis system with CNC movement (left/right and up/down) carrying a drill that grinds individual weeds out of the sward. Developed for tap-rooted weeds such as broad-leaved dock, fully chemical-free.
func_9_desc: Improving soil structure and air supply in grassland.
func_10_desc: Mowing at various heights, including 'topping' plants above ground level.
func_11_desc: Flexible arm with a brush cutter head or blades for mowing under fences and around obstacles.
func_12_desc: Pumping water from ditches for local irrigation or crop spraying.
func_13_desc: Precise application and spreading of granular fertilizers.
func_14_desc: Spreading lime to improve soil pH levels and structure.
func_15_desc: Seed box for initial crop sowing and for overseeding existing grassland in one pass.
func_16_desc: Front-mounted unit that takes seedlings out of the tray and sets them out at the right spacing.
func_17_desc: Compact seeder that spreads grass seed onto bare patches in the sward, so damaged spots close up again quickly.
func_18_desc: Even distribution of sawdust or bedding material in stables.
func_19_desc: Evenly spreading straw, specially designed for use between vegetable rows.
func_20_desc: Transporting compost within the frame structure and spreading it between the crop rows.
func_21_desc: Additional power supply modules to be installed between the frames.
func_22_desc: Generator or combustion engine mounted between the frame as an auxiliary power source for extra electricity or mechanical power.
func_23_desc: Integrated panels to extend battery life and provide sustainable power during operation.
func_24_desc: Electric motors such as the Ego Power+ or Greenworks units to drive implements that need real power, replacing small petrol engines.
func_25_desc: Large front-mounted brush or electrically driven radial brush for surface cleaning, as an alternative to the front push blade.
func_26_desc: Front or rear-mounted seat, with the option to widen the frame tubes at the sides.
func_27_desc: Motorized wheelbarrow-style bin for transporting and dumping loose materials, also usable as a carrying aid or mini dumper.
func_28_desc: Rear-mounted hitch for pulling trailers and other rolling equipment.
func_29_desc: Ballast weights to improve traction and vehicle balance for heavy tasks.
func_30_desc: External hydraulic power source for applications where hydraulics are a better option than electricity.
func_31_desc: Standard lifting system for attaching various agricultural implements.
func_32_desc: Protective enclosure or housing for the operator.
func_33_desc: Measuring grass and crop height and health to create task maps for nitrogen or phosphate.
func_34_desc: Measuring and mapping soil density at specific data points.
goal_hero_subtitle: Making complex robotics accessible by providing a solid foundation, powered by an active community of farmers and makers.

goal_feature2_desc: Thanks to electric drive and solar panel options, the robot is ideal for emission-free work in greenhouses and in the field.

robotbuild_prototype_title: From CAD Model to Working Prototype
robotbuild_prototype_alt: The Bruut prototype in a grass field with two RTK GNSS antennas on a mast
robotbuild_prototype_desc: Everything on this page has been built and driven for real. The current prototype runs on the same hole-bar chassis you see in the drawings below, with the electronics still deliberately out in the open: that way anything can be swapped, remeasured or rewired between two test runs.
robotbuild_prototype_spec_1: Two RTK GNSS antennas in a moving-baseline setup, so the robot knows its heading even when standing still
robotbuild_prototype_spec_2: Removable power-tool battery packs, a main switch and a clearly visible emergency stop
robotbuild_prototype_spec_3: Forward-facing camera on an adjustable mount for row detection and weeding trials
robotbuild_prototype_spec_4: Open deck, so every test can be logged, filmed and rebuilt the same evening
robotbuild_drive_desc: The same frame, the same brackets and the same software: only the number of driven wheels changes. Start light and cheap, and scale up when the job gets heavier.
robotbuild_drive_2wd_desc: Two driven hub motors carry the load and castors take care of the rest. This is the lightest and cheapest build, ideal for light tool work, greenhouses and gardens. It is also the configuration the prototype currently drives with.
robotbuild_drive_4wd_desc: Four driven wheels for maximum traction on soft soil and slopes. Wider track, more pulling power and room for more battery capacity for heavier implements, without changing the frame concept.
robotbuild_frame_desc: The frame is made of square tube with a repeating hole pattern. Track width and wheelbase are set by bolting the beams into a different row of holes, so the robot can be matched to your bed width or row spacing without any welding.
robotbuild_wheelunit_desc: One hub motor, two side plates and a top plate with slotted holes. The complete unit bolts onto the frame as a single module, which means swapping a motor in the field takes minutes instead of an afternoon.
robotbuild_caster_desc: The non-driven wheels of the 2WD build. They pivot freely, drop straight into the same beam and keep the robot stable without any extra electronics or control.
robotbuild_parts_desc: The brackets are built from flat sheet-metal parts that are cut and bent. All drawings are in the repository, so any local sheet-metal shop can make them, or you can cut and weld them yourself.
robotbuild_modular_desc: The robot features a highly modular framework using standard hole patterns. You can easily adjust the width, length, or height to perfectly fit specific field conditions and track widths. It's designed to be easily made and fabricated with full buildplans and pre made CNC-plans so any workshop can make it or cut and weld it yourself
robotbuild_hubmotors_desc: Powered by either 2 or 4 direct-drive hub motors (with 2 caster wheels for the 2WD setup). These maintenance-free motors provide incredible torque. Ranging from 400W to 3kW, you can scale the robot's size and capacity for heavier tasks while utilizing the exact same software.
robotbuild_maintenance_desc: Function over form: all crucial components are easily accessible through utility boxes on the robot. The system runs on a safe low-voltage battery setup (maximum 60V) with dedicated main switches. Computers and electronics are securely stored and protected inside these accessible compartments. Hardware can easily be isntalled yourself
robotbuild_customizable_desc: The open design is incredibly versatile. It can be easily expanded with a wide range of implements such as a seat, weed harrows, front blades, spray booms, or brooms, making it universally adaptable to any task.
robotbuild_control_sys_desc: Initially, the robot can be controlled via an RC remote or a built-in joystick—a vital fallback that will always remain available. The ultimate goal, however, is full autonomous operation, allowing the robot to work independently while you monitor it remotely.
robotbuild_progress_title: What We Are Testing Right Now
robotbuild_progress_desc: This is where the project stands today. Every step, including the ones that failed, is documented on the YouTube channel.
robotbuild_steering_desc: The robot started out as a dual-wheel differential drive, but that made precise line following hard to tune. It now steers as a tricycle, controlled by a pure pursuit algorithm that keeps the robot locked onto its path. The first runs went well, and the corrections that were still needed are in the videos.
robotbuild_ardupilot_desc: For RTK communication and autonomous driving we build on the open-source ArduPilot project. The robot now drives missions between AB points on its own. AB line following works, but not yet on every surface and in every turn, and that is exactly the work in progress.
robotbuild_vision_desc: A global shutter camera replaced the earlier rolling shutter setup: no more skewed frames while driving, which matters a lot for detection at speed. On top of that we use SAHI (sliced inference), which makes small objects such as young plants noticeably easier to detect.
robotbuild_steppers_desc: Implements need to move sideways and up and down, independently of the robot. NEMA 34 stepper motors are being tested for exactly that: enough torque for a side-shift frame, while staying precise and simple to drive.
robotbuild_spot_spraying_desc: Our precision spot spraying capabilities are going to be built upon the Open Weed Locator (OWL) open-source software. Innovators as Guy Coleman is what open source community makes the best
robotbuild_inrow_desc: Computer vision decides which plant stays and which one goes. There are working proof-of-concept tests for hoeing between cabbage plants in the row, for side-shift weeding, and for recognising spindle trees in nursery rows, filmed together with a tree nursery.
robotbuild_videos_cta_desc: Every build step, test drive and setback is filmed and explained. A new video appears on the channel every few weeks.
